transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-05-12 15:00 UTC | Duration: 52 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Ravi Patel (Redwood SE), Lena Ortiz (Redwood SE), Aisha Khan (Catalyst Labs - Head of ML), Tom Reynolds (Catalyst - SRE), Priya Das (Catalyst - Security), Ben Ortiz (Product)

[00:00] Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, I'm Maya from Redwood, and with me are Ravi and Lena on the engineering side, how's everyone doing?
[00:06] Aisha: Good, thanks. Appreciate you all. We wanted to walk through our migration questions, we currently run on OpenAI hosted for chat and embeddings and we're investigating dedicated/private options.
[00:12] Maya: Great, so high level is Catalyst is looking to move from OpenAI hosted to either Redwood Dedicated or Private?
[00:16] Aisha: Yes, exactly. Our drivers are cost and predictable latency, plus some data residency needs for a few enterprise customers. Also curious about running some models ourselves via vLLM and TGI stacks that we currently maintain.
[00:24] Ravi: Makes sense. Quick qualification: can you share current traffic patterns and model usage? Rough rps, typical sequence lengths, embedding volumes, that sort of thing.
[00:30] Ben: Sure. Right now we do about 40 rps on generation endpoints at peak, average seq length ~600 tokens for in-chat context, embeddings are around 2000 units per minute, and we have a heavy tail of long context sessions. We also batch some offline workloads.
[00:42] Tom: Also our SLA requirement for some customers is p95 < 450ms for short-chat flows (under 128 tokens), anything above that is a bit tricky for product.
[00:49] Lena: Okay that's helpful. When you say you maintain vLLM/TGI, are you running custom kernels or open-source model variants in-house?
[00:55] Aisha: We run a mix some fine-tuned open LLM weights on vLLM for lower-cost inference, and TGI for a couple of specialized rerankers. We want to keep that flexibility but get Redwood's runtime advantages and observability.
[01:06] Ravi: Good to hear. Two key things we usually discuss: compatibility and eval parity. For compatibility we support standard model shims, and Redwood Dedicated can host open model variants. For vLLM/TGI artifacts we can ingest model files or point to S3 locations for onboarding there's a small onboarding step to ensure kernel selection and quantization profiles are matched.
[01:24] Priya: On the security side, we need to validate KMS integrations and whether keys remain customer-managed on Private. Also SOC2, iso27001, and presence of detailed audit logs.
[01:33] Maya: Absolutely, Priya. For Dedicated we offer customer-managed KMS options with HSM support in Private. We have SOC2 Type II, and we can provide audit logs and per-request metadata. We'll share the compliance pack after the call.
[01:44] Tom: How do you handle KV cache and session state? We're concerned about cold-start overhead and token cost when a new session arrives.
[01:50] Ravi: We do continuous KV cache management in the runtime and prefix caching for common prompts. That reduces repeated full forward passes. In Dedicated, cache persistence depends on the deployment profile hot pools keep warmed caches; for Private you can configure cache sizing.
[02:02] Aisha: One suspicion from our side: we saw some output drift when we ran a model on vLLM vs OpenAI's hosted, even with the same base weights, presumably due to different kernels/quantization. How does Redwood help with eval parity?
[02:12] Lena: That's a common one. We recommend running an eval parity suite during onboarding: we take your prompt set and run it against both environments, then surface token-level diffs, score distributions, and a qualitative sample. For quantized paths we have profiles (4-bit/8-bit) and can tune them to match the full-precision baseline.
[02:28] Aisha: How much of a delta do you normally see? Is it usually acceptable for prod?
[02:33] Ravi: Typical deltas are small on generation distribution for base models if quantization is tuned, but certain safety filters or beam/temperature defaults can cause differences. We collaborate on prompt engineering and model config to minimize regression; our Optimize tooling can suggest quantization and kernel settings based on your eval metrics.
[02:48] Ben: For the POC we want to test: (1) latency at p95 for short flows, (2) end-to-end cost per 1k tokens, (3) eval parity on our 200 prompts. Is that doable?
[02:56] Maya: Yes, that's our standard POC. Ravi, can we scope a dedicated test cluster and run the customer's prompts?
[03:00] Ravi: Yep. We'll spin up a dedicated test pool with a pinned model version and run parallel against their OpenAI baseline. We'll gather latency, throughput, and token cost estimates. We'll also run TGI/vLLM artifacts if Catalyst provides the model files or we pull them from their S3.
[03:12] Priya: For deployment, network wise for Dedicated vs Private what differs? We need to know if Dedicated sits in Redwood's cloud account vs Private in our VPC.
[03:20] Maya: Dedicated is reserved capacity in Redwood-managed infra it's isolated for your tenant but runs in our accounts with private network peering. Private is the VPC/on-prem model where control plane is in Redwood but customer-managed data plane resides in your VPC or on prem. For strict compliance or air-gapped needs, Private is the path.
[03:38] Tom: If we go Dedicated, are logs and data persisted in Redwood storage? Could we enforce deletion windows?
[03:44] Maya: Yes, logs go to our observability pipeline by default; retention policies are configurable and for Dedicated we can set retention windows as contract terms. For Private you control storage entirely.
[03:53] Aisha: Pricing do you have a rough ballpark for Dedicated sizing for our numbers?
[03:58] Maya: Ballpark: for 40 rps with your seq lengths and p95 targets, it's likely a multi-GPU pool. I'll notate an estimate in the pricing doc but we'll validate after the benchmark. We also have burst options for handling spikes.
[04:11] Ben: On the technical side, are there any incompatibilities with OpenAI APIs we should expect? We have a chunk of code that assumes OpenAI response shapes and chat completion usage.
[04:19] Lena: Redwood's API is OpenAI-compatible in many ways: we support Chat and Completion-like endpoints and responses, plus function/structured outputs. There are some model name differences and optional fields we expose; we provide an SDK shim and migration guide that maps typical OpenAI calls to Redwood endpoints with minimal code changes.
[04:34] Aisha: About function calling and streaming do you support incremental token streams and function call metadata?
[04:39] Ravi: Yes, streaming is supported and we include function call annotations. Latency impact varies but it's supported end-to-end.
[04:45] Priya: For key rotation and KMS, in Dedicated, do we bring our own keys or you manage? What's the rotation policy?
[04:52] Maya: Dedicated can be configured to use customer-managed keys in supported clouds; Private, of course, gives full KMS ownership. Rotation cadence can be aligned with your policy Redwood can support automated rotation policies with minimal downtime for keys.
[05:04] Tom: Any data residency controls? We have EU customers that require data to stay in eu-west.
[05:08] Maya: Yes we have region controls and can pin Dedicated capacity to specific regions; Private gives absolute control. We'll surface region options in the sizing/pricing doc.
[05:16] Ben: Who typically owns the POC? Do we need Redwood SE to be hands-on?
[05:20] Maya: SE-led POC Ravi and Lena will run the benchmark and help interpret results. AE coordinates pricing and contract. We usually use a 2-4 week POC.
[05:29] Aisha: Timeline-wise, we want to present to our security/compliance committee in early June. Can we get SOC2 docs and an initial benchmark by late May?
[05:36] Maya: Yes, action items reflect that. We'll get the compliance pack and run the benchmark.
[05:41] Ravi: Quick technical note: if you're serving tuned models from vLLM, we recommend shipping full tokenizer and config files, and we'll match the tokenization path. That greatly reduces output drift.
[05:52] Aisha: Good to know. Also curious about multi-model routing some paths should prefer smaller cheaper models, some prefer larger. Can Redwood do policy routing?
[05:59] Lena: Yes, smart routing policies are supported route by latency SLO, cost tier, or model quality. You can define per-route fallbacks to cheaper quantized variants.
[06:10] Ben: Ok let's talk risks: what are common blockers during migrations?
[06:15] Ravi: Biggest ones: model parity causing quality regressions, underestimated capacity for tail latency, and misconfigured caching leading to higher token costs. We mitigate with an eval suite, warm pools, and Optimize recommendations.
[06:27] Priya: On legal: are there standard DPA and data flow agreements? We'll need those for procurement.
[06:32] Maya: Yes, DPA and standard procurement docs exist; I'll have legal loop in if needed.
[06:37] Tom: For observability, can we get token-level breakdowns and per-route dashboards?
[06:41] Lena: Yup, Redwood Console shows per-route latency, token counts, and cost; trace hooks can be integrated with your tracing systems.
[06:48] Aisha: Great. Any ask from us to get started?
[06:51] Ravi: Please share your eval prompt set, representative throughput profile (RPS histogram), and model artifacts (if you want us to test vLLM/TGI). A secure S3 share or signed URL works.
[06:59] Aisha: We'll get that by end of day Friday.
[07:02] Maya: Perfect. To recap next steps: Maya sends pricing and compliance docs; Ravi runs benchmark; team schedules POC kickoff for 5/22; Priya will receive SOC2 + KMS docs. Anything else?
[07:12] Ben: That covers it. Thanks everyone.
[07:15] Maya: Thanks all, we'll follow up with calendar invites and the docs.
